title: Scope, Shadowing and Linkage
quickIdea: Scope is a property of the program text: it decides which declaration a name refers to, and the nearest enclosing declaration wins. It has nothing to do with which function called which.
remember: Block scope runs from a declaration to the closing brace of its block, nested blocks included. File scope runs from the declaration to the end of the source file.
An inner declaration hides an outer one of the same name for the rest of the inner block; the outer object is neither destroyed nor changed, and it is visible again afterwards.
Function parameters have block scope that ends with the body. Redeclaring a parameter's name in the body's outermost block is a redefinition error.
C is statically, that is lexically, scoped: a name not declared locally is resolved by the enclosing text, never by the caller's frame. The latter is dynamic scoping, which C does not use.
Linkage is a separate question from scope: a file-scope name has external linkage unless declared static, and extern names an object defined elsewhere.

example.prompt: int x; void Q(int z) { z += x; printf("%d", z); } void P(int *y) { int x = *y + 2; Q(x); *y = x - 1; printf("%d", x); } main(void) { x = 5; P(&x); printf("%d", x); }
example.work: The global x is set to 5. Inside P a local x shadows it: x = *y + 2 = 5 + 2 = 7. Q is called with 7, and Q has no local x, so the name resolves to the global, still 5, making z = 7 + 5 = 12, which is printed. Back in P, *y = x - 1 writes 6 into the global through the pointer, then printf prints the local x = 7. Finally main prints the global x, now 6.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2003 Q.89 prints 12 7 6 and the marks turn entirely on which x each statement means. The same mechanism decides why a static file-scope name is invisible to other files, and why a question that says 'assume dynamic scoping' changes the answer.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: What would the same program print if C used dynamic scoping?
variations.answer: 14 7 6: Q would see P's x = 7, so z becomes 7 + 7 = 14.
variations.why: The classic paired question; it isolates scoping from everything else in the trace.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A function declares int x inside a nested block while a global x exists. Is the global reachable inside that block?
variations.answer: Not by that name - the inner declaration hides it for the rest of the block. A function without a local x still sees the global.
variations.why: Separates hiding from replacement, the distinction the 2003 question is built on.

trap.what: Assuming that a same-named local and global are one object.
trap.why: They are different objects in different storage. The local hides the global for the rest of its block, so a write to the local leaves the global untouched, and a read of the name inside that block gets the local.
trap.counterexample: int g = 1; void f(void) { int g = 2; g++; } leaves the global g equal to 1 after f returns.

check.question: What does this print? int x = 1; int main(void) { int x = 2; { int x = 3; printf("%d", x); } printf("%d", x); }
check.explanation: The innermost x is 3 inside its block; once the block ends the middle x is visible again and prints 2. The global is never printed.
